mainTopic: Leaving kosher wine made from a non-Jew's grapes in the non-Jew's property: when it stays permitted and when we worry he touched it
overview: The amud opens with the end of an earlier answer: the barrel sent into the vat is a case where the נכרי pushes it along again and again, so he may have touched the wine. Then a new משנה begins. A Jew makes kosher wine from a נכרי's grapes and leaves it in the נכרי's house that faces a public street. In a mixed city it is permitted, but in an all-non-Jewish city it needs a Jewish guard, who may come and go. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says the domain of non-Jews is all one. If the נכרי writes a receipt saying he was paid, the wine is permitted. If he holds the wine until he is paid, it is forbidden, as happened in בית שאן. The גמרא asks why an all-non-Jewish city is different, since Jewish peddlers travel everywhere, and שמואל answers that the משנה means a city with locked gates. רב יוסף adds that a window, a trash heap, or a palm tree works like a public street, and רב אחא and רבינא argue about a palm tree whose top was cut off. Finally, a ברייתא teaches that wine in a house a Jew bought or rented in a non-Jew's courtyard is permitted if a Jew lives in that courtyard, even without a key or seal.

steps.title: The barrel case: it was pushed along again and again
steps.stepSummary: The answer explains that the earlier case is one where the non-Jew keeps pushing the barrel toward the vat, so his touching is a real worry.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, the case is where it moves along from him and again from him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes an answer to a question from the previous discussion about a barrel sent into the vat. It says that case is where the non-Jew keeps pushing the barrel along.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The barrel was not thrown in one motion. The non-Jew pushed it step by step until it reached the vat. Because he stayed in contact with it the whole way, we worry he touched the wine, and that settles the earlier contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: From him and again from him, pushed by him repeatedly

steps.whatToRemember: The barrel case was a repeated push, not a single throw, so the non-Jew's contact with the wine is a real concern.

phrases.english: There,
phrases.notes: This points back to the earlier case of the barrel sent into the vat.

phrases.english: it is where it moves along by him, and again by him.
phrases.notes: He means the non-Jew keeps nudging the barrel forward instead of tossing it once.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes a question-and-answer exchange that began before this section
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It seemed the barrel case conflicted with another ruling about a non-Jew's actions
steps.terutzMaskana: The barrel case is one of repeated pushing, so the non-Jew stayed in contact with the wine

steps.title: Wine left in a non-Jew's house: mixed city versus all-non-Jewish city
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that kosher wine left in a נכרי's house facing the public street is permitted in a mixed city. In an all-non-Jewish city it is forbidden unless guarded.
steps.simpleTranslation: A Jew made a נכרי's wine kosher and left it in the נכרי's house that opens to the public street. In a city with both non-Jews and Jews, the wine is permitted. In a city that is all non-Jews, it is forbidden unless someone sits and guards it.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It rules on kosher wine that a Jew leaves in a non-Jew's house that faces a public street.
steps.deeperAnalysis: What matters is whether the נכרי is afraid of being seen. In a mixed city, Jews might walk by and catch him touching the wine, so he stays away from it. In an all-non-Jewish city he has nothing to fear, so a Jewish guard is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה, the start of a new משנה
One who makes something permitted, here by making the wine kosher

steps.confusionAlert: Here הַמְטַהֵר does not mean making something טהור from טומאה. It means the Jew prepared the נכרי's wine so that it is kosher and permitted.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One who makes a non-Jew's wine permitted,
and places it in his (the non-Jew's) domain
in a house that opens to the public street,
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets, 'and in a house'; the corrected wording, in square brackets, just says 'in a house.'

phrases.aramaic: בְּעִיר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ גּוֹיִם וְיִשְׂרְאֵלִים — מוּתָּר,
phrases.english: in a city that has non-Jews and Jews, it is permitted;
in a city that is all non-Jews, it is forbidden,
unless someone sits and guards it.
phrases.notes: Literally 'until he sits and guards.' The guard is a Jew watching the wine.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַמְטַהֵר יֵינוֹ שֶׁל נׇכְרִי, וְנוֹתְנוֹ בִּרְשׁוּתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה with a new topic
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a mixed city the wine is permitted. In an all-non-Jewish city it is forbidden unless a Jew guards it.

steps.title: The guard may come and go
steps.stepSummary: The משנה explains that the guard does not have to sit there constantly. Even if he goes in and out, the wine is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: The guard does not have to sit and guard all the time. Even if he goes out and comes back in, the wine is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה explains how strict the guarding from the previous line has to be.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nonstop watching is not required. Because the guard might walk back in at any moment, the נכרי is afraid to touch the wine. That fear is enough to keep it permitted.

phrases.english: But the guard does not need
to be sitting and guarding;

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא יוֹצֵא וְנִכְנָס — מוּתָּר.
phrases.english: even though he goes out and comes in, it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין הַשּׁוֹמֵר צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת יוֹשֵׁב וּמְשַׁמֵּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how much guarding the previous step requires
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A guard who comes and goes is enough to keep the wine permitted.

steps.title: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר: all non-Jewish domains count as one
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר gives his own short ruling: the domain of non-Jews is one.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says: the domain of non-Jews is one.
steps.whatsHappening: A תנא adds a short, puzzling statement about the non-Jew's property. The גמרא will explain what he means later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His words suggest that different non-Jewish properties should be treated the same way. The משנה does not explain how far this goes. That question is left for the גמרא.

keyTerms.meaning: The domain of non-Jews is one

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says:
The domain of non-Jews is one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a separate opinion to the משנה's ruling
steps.mimraCoreRuling: All domains of non-Jews are treated as one.

steps.title: The non-Jew writes a receipt: the wine is permitted
steps.stepSummary: If the נכרי writes the Jew a receipt saying he already received payment, the wine left in his domain is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: A Jew made a נכרי's wine kosher and left it in the נכרי's domain. If the נכרי writes him 'I received money from you,' the wine is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a second case of wine left with the נכרי, this time where the נכרי writes a receipt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The receipt shows that the נכרי treats the wine as fully belonging to the Jew. Since he sees it as someone else's property, he does not handle it, so the wine is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: And that one, meaning the non-Jew

phrases.english: One who makes a non-Jew's wine permitted
and places it in his domain,
and that one writes for him:
'I have received money from you,' it is permitted;

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַלָּה כּוֹתֵב לוֹ הִתְקַבַּלְתִּי מִמְּךָ מָעוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new case in the משנה, centered on a written receipt
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the non-Jew writes a receipt saying he was paid, the wine is permitted.

steps.title: The non-Jew holds the wine until paid: the בית שאן case
steps.stepSummary: If the נכרי will not let the Jew take the wine until he pays, the wine is forbidden, as the חכמים ruled in a real case in בית שאן.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if the Jew wants to take the wine out and the נכרי will not let him until he pays, this happened in בית שאן and they forbade it.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the opposite case and backs it up with a real event in בית שאן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the נכרי holds onto the wine as security for his money, so he feels it is still partly his. Because of that, he would not hesitate to handle it, and the wine is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: A real event that took place

steps.whatToRemember: The rule depends on how the נכרי sees the wine. If he treats it as the Jew's (he wrote a receipt), it is permitted. If he holds onto it until he is paid, it is forbidden.

phrases.english: but if the Jew wants to take it out
and he (the non-Jew) does not let him
until he gives him his money,

phrases.aramaic: זֶה הָיָה מַעֲשֶׂה בְּבֵית שְׁאָן וְאָסְרוּ.
phrases.english: this was an incident in Beit She'an, and they forbade it.
phrases.notes: 'They' means the חכמים who ruled on the case.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל אִם יִרְצֶה יִשְׂרָאֵל לְהוֹצִיא וְאֵינוֹ מַנִּיחוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The contrasting case to the receipt case in the previous step
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the non-Jew holds the wine until he is paid, it is forbidden.

steps.title: Why should an all-non-Jewish city be forbidden?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the משנה: even in an all-non-Jewish city, Jewish peddlers travel around, so the נכרי should be afraid to touch the wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: Even in a city that is all non-Jews, the wine should also be permitted. Aren't there Jewish peddlers who travel around the towns?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the משנה's line between a mixed city and an all-non-Jewish city. It says Jewish peddlers could show up anywhere, so the difference seems to disappear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a mixed city the wine is permitted because the נכרי is afraid a Jew will see him touching it. The גמרא argues that the same fear exists everywhere, because Jewish רוכלין wander from town to town. If so, the all-non-Jewish city should be permitted too.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה
Who go around from town to town

phrases.english: GEMARA:
In a city that is all non-Jews too, [it should be permitted],
for aren't there peddlers
who travel around the towns!

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעִיר שֶׁכּוּלָּהּ גּוֹיִם נָמֵי, וְהָאִיכָּא רוֹכְלִין הַמַּחְזִירִין בָּעֲיָירוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא's analysis of the משנה's first ruling from Step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that wine in an all-non-Jewish city is forbidden unless guarded
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Jewish peddlers travel to every town, so the נכרי should fear being seen there too, just as in a mixed city.

steps.title: The משנה means a city with locked gates
steps.stepSummary: שמואל answers that the משנה is talking about a city closed off with doors and a crossbar, where outsiders cannot just walk in unnoticed.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: The משנה is talking about a city that has doors and a crossbar.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל answers the challenge by narrowing the case. The forbidden all-non-Jewish city is one with gates that close.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a gated city, the residents know when outsiders come in. So the נכרי is not afraid that a peddler will suddenly see him, and the wine stays forbidden. This keeps the משנה's distinction while explaining why the peddlers do not matter here.

keyTerms.meaning: A crossbar that locks the gates

phrases.english: Shmuel said:
[It speaks] of a city that has doors and a crossbar.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: בְּעִיר שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהּ דְּלָתַיִם וּבְרִיחַ
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Peddlers can come to any town, so an all-non-Jewish city should be permitted too.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה means a gated city, where outsiders are noticed, so the נכרי has no fear and the wine is forbidden.
steps.whatToRemember: The all-non-Jewish city is forbidden only because it is closed off with gates, so the נכרי does not expect a surprise Jewish visitor.

steps.title: A window, a trash heap, and a palm tree count like a public street
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף teaches that a window, a trash heap, or a palm tree facing the wine works the same as a public street.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: A window is like a public domain, a trash heap is like a public domain, and a palm tree is like a public domain.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף adds to the משנה's rule about a house open to the public street. He lists three other things that create the same fear of being seen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה permits the wine when the house faces רשות הרבים, because the נכרי fears that people will see him. רב יוסף says the same fear comes from a window someone can look through, a trash heap that people often visit, and a palm tree someone might climb. Each one gives a chance that someone will be watching.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
And a window is considered like a public domain,
phrases.notes: He means a window that looks out onto the spot where the wine is.

phrases.english: and a trash heap is considered like a public domain,
and a palm tree is considered like a public domain.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: וְחַלּוֹן כִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the משנה's phrase 'open to the public street' and widens it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Anything that gives people a likely view of the wine, such as a window, a trash heap, or a palm tree, counts like רשות הרבים.

steps.title: Dispute over a palm tree whose top was cut off
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא and רבינא argue whether a palm tree with its top cut off still counts. One forbids, since nobody climbs a tree with no fruit. The other permits, since someone may climb it to look for a lost animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: A palm tree whose top was cut off: רב אחא and רבינא disagree about it. One forbids and one permits. The one who forbids says: why would anyone climb up there? The one who permits says: sometimes a person loses an animal and climbs up to look for it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a dispute about a special case of רב יוסף's palm tree, and then explains each side's reasoning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A palm tree counts only because someone might climb it and see the נכרי. Once the top is cut off, there is no fruit to pick, so the one who forbids says nobody climbs it and the נכרי has no fear. The one who permits says people still climb it now and then to search for a lost animal, so the fear remains.

phrases.english: [A palm tree] whose top was cut off:
Rav Acha and Ravina disagree about it:
one forbids, and one permits.
The one who forbids [holds]:
Why would someone climb up there?
And the one who permits [holds]:
sometimes a person's animal gets lost,
and he climbs up to look for it.

steps.triggerLanguage: פְּסִיק רֵישֵׁיהּ — פְּלִיגִי בַּהּ רַב אַחָא וְרָבִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the limits of רב יוסף's palm tree rule from Step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a dispute: one view forbids the wine with a topless palm tree, since nobody climbs it; the other permits, since people sometimes climb it to search for lost animals.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the whole rule depends on one question: is there a real chance someone will see the נכרי?

steps.title: Wine in a house inside a non-Jew's courtyard
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that if a Jew buys or rents a house in a non-Jew's courtyard and fills it with wine, the wine is permitted when a Jew lives in that courtyard, even without a key or seal.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: Whether someone buys or rents a house in a non-Jew's courtyard and fills it with wine, if a Jew lives in that courtyard, the wine is permitted, even though he does not have the key or a seal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a ברייתא about wine stored in a house that sits in a non-Jew's courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually a key or seal is what protects the wine from the נכרי. Here, a Jew living in the same courtyard is enough protection, because the נכרי is afraid that Jew will see him. So the wine is permitted even with no key or seal.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
Whether one who buys or one who rents
a house in a non-Jew's courtyard,
and filled it with wine,
and a Jew lives in that same courtyard,
it is permitted,

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין מַפְתֵּחַ וְחוֹתָם בְּיָדוֹ.
phrases.english: even though the key and seal are not in his hand.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֶחָד הַלּוֹקֵחַ וְאֶחָד הַשּׂוֹכֵר בַּיִת בַּחֲצֵירוֹ שֶׁל גּוֹי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: wine stored in a Jew's house inside a non-Jew's courtyard.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wine in a house a Jew bought or rented in a non-Jew's courtyard is permitted if a Jew lives in that courtyard, even without a key or seal.
steps.whatToRemember: A Jew living nearby can protect the wine just as well as a key or seal, because the נכרי fears being seen.
